one_liner: Header-only Boost sweep-line Voronoi builder for integer points and segments; beats CGAL's segment Delaunay graph, loses on points.
what_it_does: Boost.Polygon is a header-only library for integer-coordinate planar polygon Booleans, offsetting, connectivity extraction and map overlay, plus a Voronoi extension (GSoC 2010) that builds the Voronoi diagram of 2D points and non-intersecting line segments. The Voronoi API is two lines: declare voronoi_diagram<double> vd; call construct_voronoi(first, last, &vd) on any range whose element type models the Boost.Polygon point or segment concept. The output is a half-edge graph of cells, edges and vertices with floating-point vertex coordinates, and it can be traversed to get a medial axis or (as the dual) a Delaunay triangulation. It does not have CGAL's interface; inputs must be mapped to Boost.Polygon concepts or fed through voronoi_builder::insert_point / insert_segment.
how_it_is_fast: It runs Fortune's sweep-line algorithm: site events sorted once with std::sort, a beach line held in a std::map, and circle events in an ordered priority queue, O(N log N) time and O(N) memory. Robustness comes from lazy arithmetic: predicates are first evaluated in double with relative-error tracking (robust_fpt, ULP comparisons), and only when the result falls in the uncertain range do they fall back to fixed-size, stack-allocated multiprecision integers (extended_int<128> and up). The docs say this avoids multiprecision work in about 95% of cases. There is no heap new in the algorithm itself (pure STL containers).
when_to_use: Voronoi diagrams or medial axes of line segments (polylines, discretized curves, polygon outlines): the only case where the author's benchmark shows it beating CGAL, about 1.3x to 1.56x on 100 to 1,000,000 random non-intersecting segments.

You need Voronoi vertex coordinates with a guaranteed relative error bound (64 machine epsilons per the Voronoi main page; vertices within 128 epsilons are merged) rather than only a Delaunay topology.
You already depend on Boost and want no GMP/MPFR/CGAL build: the Voronoi headers need only the STL and boost/cstdint.hpp.
Inputs are, or can be snapped to, 32-bit signed integer coordinates; 64-bit or wider integers work after writing custom coordinate type traits.
Integer-grid polygon Booleans in VLSI/CAD-style workloads (Manhattan and 45-degree fast paths), where the separate polygon-set code applies.
when_not_to_use: Point-only Voronoi/Delaunay: CGAL's Delaunay_triangulation_2 was about 3.8x faster at 1,000,000 random points in this same benchmark (3.47 s vs 0.90 s), and the catalogued jc_voronoi reports about 3.65x over Boost.Polygon at 1k random sites.

Floating-point input: coordinates must be integral; you have to scale and snap, and the Voronoi builder rejects overlapping inputs (a point inside a segment, or segments crossing anywhere but at endpoints) unless you split them first with the segment utils.

Workloads that cannot tolerate open robustness bugs: open issues report an infinite loop in voronoi_diagram::_build on one 1,912-segment input (#49), missing edges with coordinates up to 10,000,000 (#43), empty cells (#47) and a bug in robust_sqrt_expr::eval2 (#41), none with a linked fix.
You need edge clipping to a bounding box, custom allocators or Delaunay output directly: none are provided (jc_voronoi's own feature table lists clipping and custom allocators as missing from Boost).

Arbitrary-angle polygon Booleans on adversarial input: the polygon-set intersection uses a divide-and-conquer heuristic that the analysis page says can go quadratic on specific inputs that defeat 1-D decomposition.

integration.dependencies: Voronoi part: STL and boost/cstdint.hpp only (Boost::config in CMake); polygon-set Booleans optionally use GMP via boost/polygon/gmp_override.hpp
integration.min_toolchain: not documented; pre-C++11 era Boost code. Open issues report C++20 warnings (#79) and a build error with a then-recent MSVC (#40)
integration.platforms: any (portable C++; 80-bit long double fpt types work on GCC but not MSVC, per the builder docs)
integration.thread_safety: not documented; voronoi_builder holds all state in member containers, so separate builder/diagram instances per thread are the safe assumption (inferred from voronoi_builder.hpp)

gotchas: Default traits support int32 input only; int64 or wider needs custom voronoi_ctype_traits, including big-int and extended-exponent float types sized per the builder page's table.
Vertices whose coordinates agree within 128 machine epsilons are merged and the edges between them dropped during finalization, so output topology can differ slightly from the exact diagram.
Segment inputs must not intersect except at endpoints, and a point must not lie inside a segment; the builder does not check this for you.
The diagram includes infinite edges (no vertex at one end); you clip them yourself for drawing or medial-axis use.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick it over jc_voronoi when sites include line segments or you need exact-predicate robustness on an integer grid; jc_voronoi is a point-only float Fortune implementation that is about 3.65x faster on 1k random points. For point-set Delaunay, pgl, Delaunay32 or CGAL itself are faster choices.
verified_claims_summary: The library author's 2013 benchmark (GCC 4.7.3, Boost 1.54, CGAL 4.3-beta1, CPU printed as 'Intel i5-7600 2.8 GHz', optimization level unstated) timed Boost.Polygon's Voronoi construction against CGAL's segment Delaunay graph and Delaunay triangulation: on random non-intersecting segments it was 25.0 s vs 39.1 s at 1M (about 1.56x) and 1.3x to 1.5x at smaller sizes, but on random points CGAL was about 3.8x faster (0.90 s vs 3.47 s at 1M). The two libraries produce different outputs (Voronoi with coordinates vs Delaunay topology), and segment-generation time is subtracted from the measured segment runs.
status_note: Stale: Boost-maintained build-system commits only (last 2025-05-02), Voronoi core unchanged since about 2013 with 41 open issues, but BSL-1.0, header-only and shipped in every Boost release, so it is easy to adopt.
